speechtext:
Shepley, K.O., was charged by the Minister of Justice with the settlement of the proposed bill and of the mortgage which is scheduled thereto. The foregoing question was accordingly submitted to Mr. Shepley by the Deputy Minister of Justice. The following is the conclusion of his formal opinion ' with which,' the Deputy Minister of Justice states, 'I quite agree.'
'The Bill introduced to provide for the loan to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company empowers the Grand Trunk Rail-

way Company to become a party to the mortgage or deed of trust scheduled to the Bill, and to enter into the contract of guaranty which the third section of the Act makes one of the securities to the government for the repayment of the proposed loan to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company.
'The guaranty referred to is fully set out in the mortgage or deed of trust, and is an unconditional contract under seal by the Grand Trunk Railway Company for the prompt payment of the principal and interest of the bonds secured by the mortgage or deed of trust.
'The second section of Article 4 of the deed of trust expressly constitutes the guaranty in question a liability of the Grand Trunk Railway Company in priority to all the share capital of that company, whether guaranteed stock, preference stock or ordinary stock.
'It is not, I think, strictly accurate to speak of either preferred share capital or the guaranty as creating a lien or charge upon the assets of the company. The preferred share capital is, under the statutes relating to it, an obligation on the part of the company towards the holders of it. Similarly, the guaranty is an obligation the non-performance of which would make the company a debtor.
'It is perfectly clear, in my opinion, that the terms of the proposed Bill and of the mortgage or deed scheduled to it, make it impossible for the company to pay dividends upon the preferred capital in priority to any debt that may arise out of the nonperformance of the guaranty. In this sense, the obligation created by the guaranty has priority over the obligation existing in respect of preferred share capital.'

subtopic: LITTLE ST. PIERRE RIVER-DRAINAGE.
LITTLE ST. PIERRE RIVER-DRAINAGE.
speechtext:
Before the Orders of the Day are called, I would ask leave to move the adjournment of the House in order to refer briefly to a definite matter of urgent public importance. Under subsection 3 of rule 37, I would state that the matter of urgent public importance is the immediate drainage and sanitation of the valley of the Little St. Pierre river. I have mentioned the matter to the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham), and if I have the necessary support of the House, I will state as briefly as I can what is urgently needed in this matter. Mr. Speaker, if this had not been a matter affecting largely the public health of the city of Montreal and its vicinity, I would have deferred the discussion until the question might be brought up in the regular course on the discussion of the estimates. But I deem it such an urgent matter and of so
much importance that I have decided, with the consent of the Minister of Railways and Canals, to bring it at once to the attention of the government and the House.
As most of the members of this House are aware, the government in building the Lachine canal, so placed that important work as to interfere materially with the drainage of an area extending from Lachine down into what was then only the outskirts of the city of Montreal. The canal follows the bank of the St. Lawrence river from one end to the other of the Lachine rapids. On one side is Mount Royal, and this canal constitutes, in reality, a kind of dyke which prevents the flow of water from a very large area, extending between the mountain and the river, to the river to which these waters would flow naturally. The effect of this was to cause, even at the very beginning, yearly floods in that part of the district of Montreal. The government, from the first, recognized that it had there an obligation of drainage, which, from time to time, it has endeavoured to satisfy, but in an imperfect manner. The administration that preceded the present one executed a work of considerable magnitude, at a cost, I believe, of over $100,000, to drain the upper part of the area just referred to. That drain was constructed in the early eighties, and it was constructed because the government recognized that the building of the canal prevented the regular flow of waters across the district. Of course, at that time the drainage and sanitation of the area was not of very great importance, because the section was very sparsely settled. There were a few farmers there, but the government arranged with many of them by paying them indemnities after arbitration on account of these periodical overflowings and the prevention of drainage. At times, I believe, the government constructed one or two conduits under the Lachine canal for the surface water; and even to-day that mode is still open to the government of preserving this area from yearly inundation lasting for a considerable time in the spring. At this time, and for a few years past, a great number of municipalities have sprung up within the limits of the undrained area, and a very large number of houses have been built, making this question of drainage and sanitation one which calls for immediate solution on the part of those who are bound to see to it that the obstacle in the way of drainage is removed. The government of Canada, either before 1896 or since that date, permitted the municipality of Lachine to empty its drainage into a main drain which started from the the upper part of Lachine and came down a considerable distance and emptied into the St. Pierre, a little Tiver which flows between the Lachine canal and the mountain, through the municipality of Notre Dame de Grace and into

the city of Montreal, and through a part of that city to the St. Lawrence. At that time the municipality of Lachine, which to-day has a population of nearly ten thousand souls, was, comparatively speaking, a small village, and the government at that time did not think it a matter of very great importance that the drainage of that village should be allowed to flow into this main drain. But since that time, as I have said, a number of important municipalities have sprung up within a short distance of this area or within its very limits. There are the municipalities of Westmount, Boulevard St. Paul, the rural municipality of Notre Dame de Grace, the municipality of Montreal West, and probably others which I am omitting. All these municipalities desire to drain into the river St. Pierre, or, if not that, to drain as far as the St. Lawrence, they are obliged to cross the Lachine canal, which is a matter of very considerable inconvenience, even if at all possible. As I have stated, the government has recognized on many occasions its share of responsibility in regard to the drainage of that area.
The provincial board of health, since more than five years, has had this question under its particular observation, and time and again has brought to the notice of the municipalities and the government the absolute urgency of draining that area in particular and the very grave objection which exists to the sewage of Lachine-a town of considerable extent and daily increasing-passing into the River St. Pierre, all along that river, and into the city of Montreal, thus forming an open drain over an extent of some 5 or 6 miles. Last year the grave danger which thus threatened these municipalities and the city of Montreal itself, induced all these municipalities, as well as the board of health, to send a delegation to interview my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals regarding the best means of putting an end to this nuisance and daily peril. To use the words of Dr. Lachapelle, the president of the provincial board of health, who formed one of this delegation, the state of affairs existing constitutes a fever nest which is a source of daily danger for nearly 400,000 people who inhabit the island of Montreal, not only in the vicinity of this exposed area but throughout the whole city and island. At any time this drain may generate fever among our population -among the poor people and also those in better circumstances who live in that immediate vicinity, whence it may extend over the city.

speechtext: Where does the River St. Pierre enter the St. Lawrence?

subtopic: LITTLE ST. PIERRE RIVER-DRAINAGE.

speechtext:
It passes through St. Gabriel ward in the city of Montreal below the canal. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways, who understood perfectly the gravity of the situation, made the suggestion, which was accepted by all the mayors and the representatives of the boards of health, and the delegation generally, that if the government had some responsibility in the matter, there was also a responsibility upon the municipalities which drained into that river or desired to do so, and that consequently all should share in the expense of devising some plan which would be submitted to the interested parties, after which a determination would be arrived at as to what should be the basis of contribution by each. That suggestion was accepted by the delegation. That was about a year ago. The government named as its expert engineer, Mr. Chipman of Toronto; the city of Montreal named Mr. Janin, superintendent of water works; and the other municipalities joined in suggesting, as their representative, Mr. Fellows, engineer of the muncipality of Westmount. It was admitted by all that the danger was immediate and increasing, and that it was absolutely necessary to proceed without delay to remove it. But that view does not seem to have been acted on by those who were charged with the preparation of plans and the devising of the best means of overcoming the difficulty. This year that area is inundated by the overflow of the St. Pierre river with all its affluent sewage and I was moved to find out what these three experts had done. In so far as I have been able to ascertain, they held one or two meetings and selected the engineer in charge of the canals of the province of Quebec to prepare some plans, and the suggestion was made that some young engineer should be employed to take levels. In order to do that some money was necessary. The municipalities contributed $600, Montreal contributed $600, the government gave $600, and a fund was constituted, and I understand that this young engineer is busy from time to time taking levels and doing some preliminary work. The object of my rising to-day is to urge my hon. friend and the government to hasten the work of these experts. My hon. friend might say that that is not more the concern of the government than of the other parties interested. I do not think it is reasonable to expect that the mayors of these municipalities would take a lively interest in this work. They cannot act without consulting their councils and without consulting among themselves, and the best proof that action on their part is difficult is shown by the fact that nothing has yet been done

practically to overcome this grave condition. On the other hand my hon. friend the minister has under his control the means of hastening the preliminary operations. His deputy is fully conversant with the situation. He has all the plans which have been made and the claims for damages, which from time to time have been produced and settled. My hon. friend has also in the canal office in Montreal the superintendent of provincial canals under his control. That gentleman is thoroughly conversant with the situation.
At any rate, whether this is more particularly my hon. friend's business or that of the other interested parties to whom I have referred, I would ask my hon. frierfd, in view of the danger attending the situation, in view of the urgency, to bring all possible pressure to bear upon these experts in order that they may finish their work and lay before the' government their report, their plans, their suggestions as to the best means of overcoming this serious difficulty without delay. My hon. friend's department, or, at any rate, the government, has undertaken very considerable work in St. Johns, in view of the rising of the St. Johns river and the flooding of the district in that vicinity. It was urged, as I understand, upon the government, that the canal there was one of the principal causes of this flood. But the district was, if I understand it aright, interested as a rural district. This is a question of doing justice to the farmers and it is a question of importance, I admit. In the instance I am now bringing to the notice of the House and of the government it is a question of the health of a very large multitude of people who undoubtedly stand in great peril of suffering and who at present suffer because the population is becoming more dense all the time. To children playing on the shores of this little river the danger is continuous, and the prevalence of fever there has been most marked. Under these circumstances I think my hon. friend should take the matter in hand, and I have no doubt that if he brings pressure to bear upon the experts I have named he will have the report without delay and that the work will be undertaken immediately, because once that report is before my hon. friend and the interested parties there will undoubtedly be an agreement as to the proportion of the cost of the work to be borne by each. I agree with the suggestion that I have heard more than once made during the present session in this House that it is during the time of depression that public works should be executed. There is no doubt at the present moment we have in the city of Montreal, as well as in other large cities of this Dominion, a very large number of unemployed people. They could not be better employed than this. The only thing that is necessary is to make the ex-134
perts understand the urgency, the gravity of the situation, as depicted to us by the provincial board of health, call for tenders and have this work executed without delay. I beg to move the adjournment of the House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question of public health is a paramount one, one that deserves the attention of this House and I have listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). I understand the importance of the question he has discussed. Some months, or perhaps a year ago, this matter, as outlined by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, was brought to my attention and steps were taken along the lines indicated by him. But this much ought to be remembered, that this is not a government work. My hon. friend rather assumes the position that the government has undertaken the drainage of this section of Montreal. That is not the position. The question of public health lies wholly with the, provincial and municipal authorities. If this government be liable for any act it ought to be prepared to meet that liability. It was along the lines of sympathy for the grievances of the residents in this locality that the question was approached. It was asserted that the government had become responsible to a certain extent by allowing the sewage of Lachine to pass through a certain sewer. The conditions at that time were altogether different. We did not have any of these smaller municipalities that have grown up in that particular locality. In discussing the question, feeling the responsibility and the gravity of any situation that would militate against the health of the people, I felt that it was the duty of this government, if it had any liability, to meet it in reference to the matter. I agreed readily on the part of the government to appoint an engineer to associate himself with the engineers that the municipalities and the province might appoint to look into the matter, but, mark you, the Department of Railways and Canals did not assume this as a government work. The work, if carried out as it ought to be, and the protection of the public health, lie wholly in the hands of the provincial and municipal authorities themselves under the board of health regulations and under the provincial Municipal Act. As a party, if it be a party, the government is prepared to do its share towards the remedying of the grievance. Just what the engineers have done I am not prepared to say, as my hon. friend's note was just handed to me a few minutes ago. The city of Montreal surely is the party really interested. These smaller municipalities in which this state of affars is said to exist, certainly form the community that is really interested, but the pro-



vincial board of health, having charge of the health of the people, is certainly deeply interested, and if this government is prepared to pay any share of the liability that may appear as belonging to it and to perhaps act generously in that regard, certainly, it is doing all that it is called upon to do. We are prepared to do that and perhaps to be a little generous along that line, but I would not like my hon. friend to retain the idea that this government ought to undertake it as a public work. It is a purely local or municipal work for the protection of the public health. As far as we are liable this government and this parliament ought to meet that liability and we will gladly do so. I will call the attention of the officers of my department to the remarks of my hon. friend, and I will see in what position the report of this board is, what they have done and what they have placed before the department as the result of their labour.

subtopic: LITTLE ST. PIERRE RIVER-DRAINAGE.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am pretty thoroughly acquainted with this question, as the circumstances which have been alluded to occurred when I was managing the Department of Railways and Canals. The liability of the government in reference to this particular affair is that we, in constructing the Lachine canal, rendered it almost impossible for the people of Lachine to drain that municipality without passing the drain under the Lachine canal. The liability of the government with respect to that was assumed long ago. We built a drain along the Lachine canal, built works under the Lachine canal for the purpose of draining this particular locality, and I think we deepened the St. Pierre river from the Lachine canal down to_ the city of Montreal. The extent of the liability of the government is confined to this: How much more difficult have we made it for the people to drain that municipality for the purposes of sanitation than it was before? It was nearly impossible for the people of Lachine to drain under the mouth or entrance of the canal. There was no way but by building a ditch alongside of the Lachine canal and putting culyerts under the canal for the purposes of drainage. The government, rightly or wrongly, assumed that work and allowed the people of Lachine to drain under the canal; in fact, it was built for no other purpose than for draining the village of Lachine. When we got under the canal we found that we were lower than the bed of the St. Pierre river and we were obliged to deepen the St. Pierre river from the Lachine canal down to Montreal. When we built the Lachine canal we made it impossible for those on the north side to have drainage without a drain underneath the canal, and for that reason the government is bound to see that all reasonable and safe facilities are

Resolved, That it is expedient to amend the Post Office Act and the Civil Service Act and to provide as follows:-
That in the outside division of the Post Office Department the salaries of messengers, porters, letter-carriers, mail transfer agents or box collectors shall, in Grade A he at the rate of $1.75 per day, in Grade B at the rate of $2.00 per day, in Grade C at the rate of $2.25 per day, in Grade D at the rate of $2.50 per day, in Grade E at the rate of S2.75 per day; that the salaries of the fourth-class clerks shall, on appointment, be $500 with annual increases of $100 up to $700 ;

speechtext:
I wish to give a very brief explanation of this resolution. The salaries of letter-carriers are fixed by the Post Office Act and the salaries of the fourth-class clerks by the old Civil Service Act so that both will require to be amended. Since I took office, and during many years previously, representations have been made to the Postmaster General and to the government, by commercial bodies, by municipal councils and other representative institutions, not to speak of members of parliament on both sides, asking that the salaries of the letter-carriers should be increased. In 1902 Sir William Mulock, then Postmaster General, increased the salaries of the letter-carriers to some extent. Two years ago, the commission appointed to inquire into the Civil Service included in their report the following recommendation:
Your Commissioners find that a few years ago the laws regarding the employment of letter-carriers were considerably altered. The letter-carrier was changed from an official drawing a yearly salary to an official drawing a daily salary, and in cases of absence through sickness or otherwise, deductions of pay were enforced. No doubt in the best interests of the service these laws require to be rigidly enforced. Nothing comes so much into the daily life of the community as the delivery of the mail. It is a service requiring prompt and efficient action. In certain places favouritism is alleged on the part of high officials towards certain letter-carriers who were allowed leave of absence with pay, but others of the same euass were fined. Your Commissioners do not, however, think this worthy of attention, but they are of opinion that it would be desirable as far as possible to bring the services of letter-carriers to an eight-hour a day service. They would also suggest an additional week's leave of absence be allowed this branch of the service, and on consideration they recommend that at least the schedules of salaries laid down by Mr. Ross, Superintendent of Post Offices, should be adopted. Mr. Ross has filed an extensive memorandum which is to be found appended to his evidence.
I -may say that the resolutions now before the House are based on the report made by Mr. Ross chief superintendent, and a higher official of the Post Office service. The present scale of salaries paid to letter-carriers is provided for in sections 39 and 40 of the Act, and the same scale prevails in the smaller cities as well as the - larger cities, wdierever the system of free delivery exists. Briefly, the scale of salaries is as follows:	In grade A, on entermi	i
ing the service, during a probationary period of one month, a letter-carrier is paid $1.25 per day. If the man is found sufficiently well equipped, intellectually and morally, at the expiration of the probationary month, he is immediately put into grade B at $1.50 per day.

The Post Office Department furnishes uniforms, boots and helmets. In addition, in the large cities we give letter-carriers in uniform free transportation on the street cars, for which we pay a fixed sum to the Street Railway Company. Under the proposal before the House, if the resolution carries, letter-carriers, during their first month, the probationary period, instead of receiving $1.25

per day, will hereafter receive $1.75; after their probationary period, in the first, year, instead of $1.50, they will receive $2" per day. In the second year, instead of $1.50, they will receive $2 per day. In the third year, instead of $1.75, they will receive $2.25. In the fourth year, instead of $2.25, they will receive $2.50, or, for specially arduous duties or specially long runs, $2.75 per day'. The rate of pay attached to each grade is proposed to be increased 50 cents per day. But the great advantage, in my mind, is that a letter-carrier, from his entrance into the service, receives sufficient for the maintenance of himself and his family in a fairly adequate manner. I need not refer to the representations that have been made to the government and to the members individually by the letter-carriers and their many friends in the country. I freely admit that under the old system they did not receive enough to maintain themselves properly, with the increase in the cost of living during the last ten years, and even during the last five years.

speechtext:
When Sir Wm. Mulock introduced his amendment to the Post Office Act by which he brought letter-carriers under the grade system and increased their pay, many of the old letter-carriers refused to come under that /system although they received less pay under the former one. The object of the amendment Mr. LEMIEUX.
was not only to increase the pay, but to obtain better service. Under the old Act many of the letter-carriers were subject to malingering or simulation of illness. They knew they would be paid in any event, and frequently were indisposed much to the detriment of the service. But under the grade system a man is paid for every day of work. If absent he is not paid unless he satisfies the authorities that he has been the victim of an accident while on duty or was really suffering under serious illness contracted in the service. We thus put a brake on what was really an abuse, and we notice that to-day we have, practically speaking, no more absentees. The letter-carriers are scarcely ever absent and avail themselves of the annual leave of twenty days with pay. On three different occasions Sir Wm. Mulock extended the delay given the old letter-carriers to come undeT the grade system, and nearly all of them did so. But about 75 or 80 have refused up to date, and in order that they may benefit by the new increase we shall have to make further amendments.

I am glad, however, that my hon. friend has called my attention to this matter, and will look into it, as I do not wish to take advantage of the disadvantageous position under which these letter-carriers agreed to remain since many years.

speechtext: Does the hon. minister really think that $1.75 per day is sufficient pay for these men when they start in? In our city $2 per day is about the smallest wage a common labourer gets. If you would increase the minimum to $2 per day and the other grades by 25 cents per day, that would be none too much, considering the extra cost of living. Civil servants were under a certain schedule for many years and no doubt when this increase is made fit will remain in force a number of years to come. It would not be unjust to give these men $2 a day to start with, as no man with a family can save much on that wage and live in decency and comfort.

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext:
It is easy to suggest that the letter-carriers should receive $2 a day at the start instead of $1.75, but the present increase will cost the country $200,000 per annum in round numbers, so that we must be careful. I shall, however, take a note of what my hon. friend has said. No doubt some other hon. members will argue in

favour of a larger increase, but the money is not my own, but that of the people, and whilst I would be pleased to give $4 or $5 per day to every man employed in the departments, yet I have to keep within limits. On the whole, the letter-carriers are satisfied with the increase given them at present. Judging by the' deputations I have received since I have been in office, this amount is considered as fairly adequate to the exigencies of the present day.
To come to the fourth class, the stampers, sorters and other lower grades, their pay is governed by the old Civil iServiee Act, which was wiped out from the statute-book as regards the inside service, but still Temains as regards the outside service. According to the Civil Service Act, the fourth-class clerks are treated as follows:
The minimum salary attached to a fourth-class clerk, the lowest clerkship in the service, is $400 per annum
The fourth-class clerk enters the service at $400 a year, and by annual increases of $50 reaches a maximum of $700 a year. We found that young men entering the service under these conditions remained a few months, perhaps a year or so, but, when they had become fairly efficient clerks, they left the service. This was rehearsed every year in that class of our employees. The fourth-class clerks are not sufficiently paid when they enter the service, and therefore they almost invariably leave when they find an opportunity. We believe that they should receive from the beginning a salary of not less than $500, and should reach their maximum by annual increases of $100 instead of $50.
Now, as regards stampers and sorters- and this class must be differentiated from the fourth-class clerks-I recommend that they should receive, at the beginning, $500 a year, instead of $360 a year, as at present, and should receive annual increases of $50 instead of $100, because their functions are of the simplest nature so that they are not to be considered as of the same degree of usefulness as are the fourth-class clerks. Their maximum should be $600 per annum!. When they reach this maximum they will be eligible for promotion at once to the position of fourth-class clerk, beginning in that class at a salary of $600, at which they leave the class of stampers and sorters. That is, let us say, a stamper comes into the service in Montreal at $500; after two years he reaches
his maximum of $600. If he has given good service, he is promoted to the position of fourth-class clerk at a salary of not less than $600, and goes on by annual increases of $100 to the maximum of that class, $800.
Such are the changes I propose in these resolutions. I may say, in conclusion, that these increases will affect the salaries of 1,500 men in round figures, throughout the length and breadth of this country, and that the amount involved in these increases is estimated at $217,880.50.

speechtext:
I congratulate my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux? on having rendered justice, to a certain extent, to the Post Office employees. Their claims have been neglected for a very long time. I do not know of any class of public employees-judging by those in Montreal- who perform their duties more creditably or under greater hardship. People generally do not realize what a difficult business is the carrying of letters in a city like Montreal. The loads they have to carry are heavy, they have to face the weather whatever it may be, and, owing to the number of tenements in the city, they have to do a great deal of climbing. In view of the nature of their work, I think they have been, up to now, insufficiently paid, and my hon. friend is rendering them a bare act of justice in this increase. But I wanted to support what was stated by my hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. A. C. Macdonellj a moment ago. I think that a man who fulfils carefully the duties of a letter-carrier in a city like Montreal ought to begin with the remuneration of not less than $2 a day. It seems to me that, in that regard, my hon. friend the Postmaster General might well make a distinction between large cities like Montreal and Toronto, and smaller cities in which free delivery is carried on. The Postmaster General stated in the House the other day that any town that gave the government a postal revenue of $20,000 and Bad a population of 10,000 was entitled to free delivery. It is evident that in a town of ten thousand inhabitants, the cost of living is very much less than in a city like Montreal or Toronto. As soon as you begin to live in one of these cities you must face at once a heavy item of expense in rent and taxes. For this reason, it seems to me, a beginner in a big city who carefully fulfils the duties of this position should receive an indemnity of at least $2 a day. Without dwelling on the matter at length, I would urge my hon. friend to consider whether, in these larger cities, $2 a day ought not to be the minimum to the beginner. A man who has a family, and is in a position of trust of this kind and has so much work to do, ought not to have less than this sum. Another point to which I wish to call attention was referred to by my hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell). I do not think that the government ought to penalize those who have availed themselves of the option given to them by Sir William Mulock, to remain under the old Act. Representations have been made to me by several of these employees in Montreal. I regret that I have not their letters with me. They remained under the old Act, and therefore are not graded. They are receiving $400, $500, or $600 a year, being paid
by the year and not by the day. There was nothing wrong about their availing themselves of the offer of Sir William Mulock. I am sure my hon. friend will find some way of getting over the difficulty, because these employees have performed their duties as well as the graded employees have done, and surely they are entitled to the same increase. I hope my hon. friend will be able, particularly in regard to that class, to render justice, and put them in the same position as the others

speechtext:
Like the hon. gentleman from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), I am glad to see this measure, though belated, brought down by the Postmaster General. It deals with a class of employees, who, in the past, in my opinion, have had very insufficient pay. Their duties are arduous; it is unnecessary to dilate upon them, because I think the Postmaster General has a thorough appreciation of their duties. The scale of increases is not large, though it is certainly a great improvement on their present position. I do not think, however, in considering what they are justly entitled to, that it is fair to consider only what they have been receiving in the past. What they have been receiving is but a modicum of what they are entitled to. I think it would be fairer to have regard to the services they perform, and to the compensation which men of their education and competency receive in other avenues of life. I certainly concur in a remark made a few moments ago that no person, no ablebodied man, educated and intelligent as a postman must be, should receive less, when he is permanently employed, than $2 a day. I trust the Postmaster General will consider that point before the Bill is brought down, and that he will treat them, having regard, not to what they have been receiving already, but to what in all human decency they are entitled to receive. I would also emphasize the remark of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), that men in large cities like Toronto and Montreal, performing the duties of postmen, are entitled to a higher rate of pay than men living in small places where the expense of living is much less than it is in large cities. We should also keep in mind that the duties of postmen in large cities are much more arduous than they are in a village or town. In the first place they have to be men of high intelligence in order to find the location of people to whom the letters are addressed, and they have to carry a class of letters generally of more value, registered letters, and they are consequently burdened with greater responsibility than postmen in country places

where they usually carry only ordinary correspondence.
Now with regard to what I mentioned a moment ago, namely, letter-carriers who are under the old Civil Service Act, I trust the minister will take this opportunity, not only of doing justice to a class of men who are now discriminated against, but also of simplifying and making uniform the entire letter-carrier service of the country. At the present time, I am informed there are only 80 letter-carriers who are under the . old Civil Service Act, and as long as they remain under that Act you will have a dual system.

speechtext: They would not join the new system.

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: They were given an opportunity of either joining the new system or of taking their status under the old system. An hon. member well says that the door ought to be still left open for them to join in the new system. I think they should be given another opportunity now, and I apprehend the minister will afford these men an opportunity, if they so desire, of coming in under the new grade system. There is a special reason for it now. Some men are receiving 50 cents a day more, and having regard to their changed condition, it would be fair, in my opinion, that those men who are under the old Civil Service Act should be given another opportunity of coming under the grade system. I am informed that the maximum those men now receive is $600 a year, that no man under the old Civil Service Act can receive more, or earn more, than $600 a year. Now these men who are under the old system are old men, old in the service, they have proved their competency by many years of faithful service, and I think they should be given an opportunity of coming into a class with the graded men. It would certainly seem to be in the public interest to have uniformity with regard to the employment of civil servants in this department. I hope that before the Bill is brought down the minister will be able to make such changes as will, if not reduce all men to a uniform and simple basis, at least give the men who are under the old Act an opportunity of being graded with the other men.-

Not only ought we to try to keep our Civil Service on the pay basis, to make them fairly independent, but we ought also to surround them with such safeguards that they may not be led to look to what we call political Mr. MACDONELL.
pull for the maintenance of their position, or for preferment. I would like the minister to think that matter over. We will also discuss the case of those men who, having twice had an opportunity of making their choice, have not all made it, and I am sure the minister will arrange that the door may still remain open, and that they may have another opportunity in that respect.

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: I would like to add a word of encouragement to the Postmaster General to treat with greater generosity as well as justice the class of men who are under consideration. Certainly we are all agreed in recognizing that they are entitled to better treatment. I would like to join the hon. members who have preceded me in urging upon the minister the importance of considering whether the minimum wage for letter-carriers should not be somewhat increased. Speaking for my own city of Montreal, I think that anybody who sees the work these letter-carriers have to perform, and who realizes the degree of intelligence they must possess in order to perform their duties- satisfactorily, must agree that $2 a day is very small compensation in view of the responsibilities which rest upon them. I have the advantage of knowing a large number of this class of employees in the city of Montreal, and particularly in my own constituency, I have observed the diligence with which they perform their duties, and I desire to commend them to the most favourable consideration of the Postmaster General when he arranges the scale of salaries in this Bill. I hope he will see his way to make the pay at all events somewhat larger than is proposed.

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: I would like to add my expression of appreciation of the proposals made by the Postmaster General. The only suggestion I would like to make is one that has already been mentioned by other hon. members, that is, that the minimum should be $2 per day instead of $1.75. I understand the Postmaster General proposes to pay $1.75 for the first year, $2 the second year and $2.25 for the third. Now, rather than place them at $1.75 at the start I would prefer that they should receive $2 per day from the beginning, and that it should remain at that for two years, and that the increase should not commence until the third year, rather than restrict them to $1.75 the first year. I quite agree with my hon. friend who has just spoken that $2 a day is the very lowest that any one could undertake to live upon.

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext:
My hon. friend unavoidably makes a mistake there. At present the letter-carrier, during his probationary period, receives $1.25 a day. That lasts one month and then he receives $1.50 per day. Under the proposed scale he will receive, during his probationary period of

one month, $1.75 per day and then he will receive $2 per day.

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: When is it proposed that the increase shall date from?

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: When the House prorogues.

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: It is only one month of probation instead of one year?

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: Who gets the gross sum-but we are gradually eliminating this system because of the grave complaints against some of the postmasters. However, it is a matter which requires departmental action and not legislation. The attention of the government has been called to it by several of the members who happen to represent some of those cities which are under the semi-staff system and action will be taken in due course upon the matter.

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: One month of probation.

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: Will the minister tell us what the estimated increased cost to the department will be and whether he has taken into consideration the clerks that are under the postmasters in different towns? I have called attention on several occasions to the small salaries that are paid to clerks who are under the postmasters in small towns and I would like to ask the minister whether he is making any provision for these clerks?

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: As to the increase in the cost of the service I gave to 'Hansard' a moment ago a statement which I did not read, but, in round figures the annual expenditure involved in this increase is $217,000. That will affect the salaries of about 1,500 employees. As to the other question brought up by my hon. friend and as to the condition in some of the cities where they have the letter system but where they are on the semi-staff basis, I may say that the letter-carriers will benefit by this increase just as the letter-carriers in the larger cities will. The clerks in these offices will not be affected however. My attention has been called, especially by the hon. member for Essex and by the hon. member for Brant, to the subject. The question is now before the department. No legislation is needed to bring these offices under the general rule and to place them on the Civil Service list. It is departmental action that is required in each case.

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: Which offices is the hon. gentleman speaking about?

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: I mean offices like Brantford, Windsor, Fort William, Sarnia, offices in cities where they have a population of not less than 12,000 and a revenue of not less than $20,000.

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: Does not this Bill aply to those letter-carriers?

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: Yes. The letter-carriers in these cities will benefit by this increase. But my hon. friend (Mr. Armstrong) referred to clerks in these offices. The clerks in many of these offices are hiTed by the postmasters.

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: Who gets the gross sum?

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: I understand there is no exception in regard to letter-carriers, that this Act will apply to all?

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: All come under the same rule.

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: As to the matter which my hon. friend has mentioned, I rather agree with my hon. friend from East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) that the system in some of these post offices where the postmaster gets the gross sum and pays what he likes to the clerks is not fair to them. They naturally do not want to complain and lose their positions and yet they do not know what their rights are and do not get their rights. I know that a great many are underpaid and I believe that something should be done to see that these postmasters who get the gross sum are at least required to pay according to some rule so that there will be some check upon the amount they pay these men who do all the work in these offices. In most cases the postmaster does nothing but the bossing and the receiving of the salary. The laborious part of the work is done by these men who have to take what he chooses to give them or else give up the work entirely.

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: I am satisfied that if the Postmaster General will investigate the conditions in the towns having a population of 5,000 and up to 12,000, he will find in many instances that the clerks who are working in these offices get a mere pittance for the amount of labour they do. I would ask the Postmaster General, when he comes to discuss the Bill in committee, if he would be good enough to explain why the cost of the delivery of the mail and of general postal facilities in the Yukon was $127,000 while the income from all sources apparently in that country only amounted to about $14,000 and whether the increased amount will be paid to the civil servants in that part of the country. I would also ask him to be good enough to explain, when the Bill is in committee, why it is that in the city of Montreal the contingent expenses last year amounted to $52,000 and in Ottawa to ' $60,000, while in Hamilton they only amounted to $4,000, London $5,000, Halifax $2,000, Quebec $5,000, Toronto $29,000 and Winnipeg $17,000.

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext:
Without going into details, but speaking from memory as regards the Yukon, from the beginning of . the establishment of the postal service in that far away district, the amount has always been the same. The revenue is somewhat limited, more limited now than it was during the rush period because the population has decreased as my hon. friend is well aware. But the reason why it costs so much money is on account of the distance and the difficulties in performing the service. We have to pay what I call an enormous amount of subsidy to one railway company. That railway company practically ties the hands of the government because it has the only railway between Whitehorse and Skagway. Between Skagway and Dawson again there is only one steamship company on the lakes in summer and in winter that same company performs the sleigh service. If the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Congdon) were in his seat he would inform my hon. friend that what can be purchased for one dollar in this section of the country costs $5 or $6 in that district. My hon. friend referred to the amount paid for contingencies in the Montreal post office, for instance. We have been obliged to employ a somewhat greater number of men in Montreal than in Toronto, although the revenue of the Toronto post office is higher than that of Montreal. In Montreal the ocean mail is made up for the different parts of the country and as there is more mail for the west than for the east we require a larger force there. My hon. friend may rest assured that we do not overload the service in Montreal. On the contrary,
I resist as much as possible demands made by the Montreal postmaster and by his very able assistant.

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: That should not apply to Ottawa.

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: Well, hitherto men have been presumably employed in the Ottawa post office and paid out of contingencies when as a matter of fact they were working in the inside service. That of course would be remedied by the new Act.

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: Are the railway mail clerks affected by this Bill?

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext:
No. This is a year of retrenchment and we must provide for the most-I will not say the most deserving- but we must provide for the most appealing cases first. I freely admit that the railway mail clerk performs very arduous duties and has many difficulties to encounter especially that of securing insurance owing to the hazarduous nature of his employment. He enters the service at a salary of $400 per year for the first six months and then he gets $500 a year in addition to his mileage of one cent per mile in the night time and half a cent per mile in the day time. He increases Mr. ARMSTRONG.
rapidly until he gets $1,200 salary in addition to his mileage. That is a fairly good salary. I do not say it is an extraordinary salary or that the railway mail clerk is not deserving of more, but in view of the retrenchment we are practising this year I thought we should take the most deserving cases first. I have received several delegations from the railway mail clerks during the last two or three years and I may say that they have my warm sympathy. When the proper time comes I will see that they receive not cold justice but warm justice.

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: How long is it since the railway mail clerks had their salaries increased?

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: In 1903, when Sir Wm. Mulock was Postmaster General. My hon. friend must remember that they reach a maximum of $1,200 a year in addition to their mileage so that some of them receive $1,800 a year. I recognize however that they have to perform difficult and arduous duties.

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: What has the population of a town got to be so that the clerks in the post office are paid directly by the government and not by the postmasters out of their revenue? In many cases these postmasters put boys and girls into the post office and give them hardly enough to live on. In many of these small towns the postmaster receives quite a large income out of which he has to pay two or three clerks but he gives them so little that he cannot secure persons capable of doing the work and consequently the public service suffers.

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: There is no fixed departmental rule but the custom of late years has been to put on a semi-staff basis the offices which have approximately an annual revenue ranging between $20,000 and $25,000. In some cases places with a small population will contribute more to the postal revenue than others where the population is larger so that population cannot be taken as a test, I have received representations on this matter, especially from the membets from Essex and the member for Brant and it is under the very serious consideration of the department. Some postmasters are really not acting as they should, because they receive a very nice salary and they under pay their clerks. The representations under that head have been so strong that the department intends to put an end to the grievance.

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext:
I hope the hon. minister will not forget that matter, because it is very important and very urgent. In many cases postmasters who receive a large enough salary to enable them to pay their assistants a fair remuneration, pay them as low as $200 a year and sometimes less. The

result is that the public is not served as it should be. The government should look into that matter without delay.

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: I want to congratulate the minister on bringing down this Bill and doing this measure of justice, even though it is a little late. I wish to draw his attention to the fact that the cost of living in a city like Winnipeg is at least 25 per cent greater than it is in a city like Ottawa, and I ask him if he is making any provision for giving the Manitoba letter-carriers a greater increase than those in Montreal or Ottawa, so as to put them on an equal footing.

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: We do recognize the fact that the cost of living is higher in the west than in the east, and every year a provisional allowance is voted and paid pro rata to all our employees in the west, including Winnipeg.

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext: One other point I wish to refer to. There are in Winnipeg a number of men who do not come in under the old Act, and I think it would be a great hardship if the door were now closed upon them, and they were prevented from coming in under the new classification.

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK CENTRAL RAILWAY -REPORT OF PROVINCIAL COMMISSION.
speechtext:
I think the railway mail clerks are as much entitled to an increase as the other civil servants. Their work is of a dangerous character and they require to be clerks of a superior class. It is some six or seven years since they have had an increase, and I think they are now entitled to a flat increase of $150 or at least $100 a year. I would ask the minister to consider their case before he brings in a Bill.

S. Mayes, a contractor of that city. That affidavit was read by the premier of the province of New Brunswick in a very large and crowded mass meeting, of citizens during the election contest then taking place.

When this matter was referred to in the House before, you distinctly stated, Mr. Speaker, that it was out of order. If it was out of order then, surely it is in order now.

What is your ruling?

I propose to offer a resolution, and one that I think will be quite in order. I had hoped that the government itself would have thought this matteT to be of sufficient importance for themselves to have taken it up in the same way that they took action in the Hodgins matter last year. In order to refresh the memory of hon. members, I may state that on the 24th day of April, 1908, the Right Hon. the Prime Minister stated in this House that he had received from Mr. Parent, the chairman of the Transcontinental Railway Commission, the following papers, wmch he desired to lay before the House. The first was a letter from Mr. Parent, addressed to the Prime Minister, in which Mr. Parent says:
A letter from Major Hodgins, lately our district engineer in northern Ontario, has been given wide publicity in the press, namely, by the Manitoba 'Free Press and the Ottawa 'Morning Citizen/ where it was o( mmented on. There are insinuations and statements in it that should not be allowed to nass unanswered. Without laying any specific charges. Major Hodgins makes vague, general accusations that are absolutely groundless. It is plain that the object in liew is to cause us annoyance'without any regard to truth or public interest.
Then, Mr. Parent goes on and concludes as follows:
In conclusion the commissioners would respectfully request, as they do not wish to remain under the aspersions which such reports pass on them, that the whole matter be referred to and looked into by a committee of the House and that Major Hodgins be assigned to appear before the same and repeat his charges in a specific manner in order to substantiate them if he can.
The action taken by the right hon. the Prime Minister on that letter consisted in

his moving the following resolution on the 27th of April, a few days later:
That the memorandum of the chairman of the Transcontinental Commissioners to the Prime Minister dated 23rd of April and laid on the table the 24th of August and the papers accompanying the same be referred to a special committee of five members with instructions to investigate the matters and charges therein mentioned and that the said
committee be composed of	and that they

They were afterwards given power to examine witnesses under oath. That is the action which I thought the government would have taken in this case, for it appears to me that the two cases are on all fours, with this exception that what Major Hodgins did was simply to write a letter containing statements which Mr. Parent thought -were not true, reflecting on himself and his co-commissioners, and therefore should be investigated. In that case there was simply a letter written by Major Hod-gins, but in the case I am now referring to we have the solemn declaration or affidavit of Mr. Mayes.

Yes, I have it.
Would my hon. friend be good enough to allow me to read it while he is speaking.

I shall read it. It is as follows:
I, Gershon S. Mayes, of the parish of Lancaster, in the city and county of St. John, in the province of New Brunswick, contractor, do solemnly declare:- That on the 1st of September, 1905, on the advice of the Hon. Wm. Pugsley, then Attorney General of the province of New Bi unswick, and now Minister of Public Works of Canada, I had a conversation with Mr. Geo. McAvity, of the city of St. John, in the said province, merchant, relative to tenders for dredging which was then to be dene in the harbour of St. John by the Public Works Department of Canada, of which the Hon. C. S. Hyman was then minister. Mr. McAvity proposed that I should go to Ottawa on Monday, the 4th of September, as he was going, and he would meet me up there at the Kussell on the 5th inst. We did meet according to appointment. Mr. McAvity wrnted to know what price I wanted. I told him I had tendered in June for 50 cents per cubic yard. He said, why not ask 55 cents and give him (McAvity) 5 cents per yard or 10 per cent. I said, why not do as we talked of at St. John, which was that he should go in

with me and take one-quarter or one-half the cost of the dredge and receive his proportion of the profits. He said, yes, he could do that when he got home and might put $10,000 to $20,000 into it and perhaps get some friends in it with him, but for the present he would go in on a percentage basis and would see Hyman right away. Well, I said, what would I do about financing it and what was he going to do to help me. Oh, he said, you can easily arrange with the banks; no trouble at all when you have got the contract. We went to see Mr. Hyman at 2.30 p.m. McAvity went in and I stayed outside. I had told McAvity to arrange if possible to have at least 400,000 yards to dredge. Mr. McAvity came out and got me to go in, and I explained to Mr. Hyman the difficulty of bringing a big plant and only dredging a small quantity. Mr. Hyman agreed to see that if I got the contract- that is if I was the lowest tenderer-I should receive 400,000 yards. Afterwards McAvity said I had better arrange an agreement. I said why not wait until we get back to St. John to hear whether my tender has been accepted or not. He said he had a copy of the agreement all ready. I said, how did he get it? He said, oh, they were all ready here. I then read it over and told him it was all one-sided; I was to do the work, he was to get the profit. Well, he said, what do you want me to do? I told him I still thought he should be financially interested he and his friends, to the extent of some $20,000 or $30,000 at least, that it was a long back load for me to carry. Oh, he said as before, the banks would help me and wait until I got home. No, I said, I have got to go right to Boston and close a contract with the dredge-owners. Well, he said, better sign the agreement. No, I said, he should be bound to do something. He said for me to write something at the bottom and he would sign it. I said I was not a lawyer. Oh, go ahead, he said, and I wrote what came to me and he signed it.
The next day I was informed by Mr. Hyman that my tender was accepted, and months afterwards I learned that mine was the only tender received. The engineer of the department wrote me a letter giving 400,000 yards to be done, and I left for Boston via Montreal and afterwards secured a dredge and brought her to St. John.

It seems to me wre are wandering a little afield in this lengthy discussion. The motion before the House is that Mr. Speaker should leave the chair for the House to into committee of supply and there is no better understood constitutional principle that on such a motion the people should have a right to air their grievances and that the members of this House have the right to say anything within the bounds of parliamentary propriety at such a time. Whether or not a motion is to be made is a matter of utter indifference. It is true that in this case the hon. gentleman who intends to make a motion has put the motion in the hands of Mr. Speaker, but that after all is a matter of private courtesy between the member and Mr. Speaker. The question is whether or not the hon. member who had the floor was out of order when the point of order was raised by the 136J
Minister of .Public Works. In fact two points of order were raised, one by the Minister of Public Works and one by the leader of the House. The point taken by the Minister of Public Works, as I under stand it, is, that there was something that would contravene rule 19, not in what was about to be said but in what had been said by the hon. member. I submit that rule 19 has no application to the future; it applies only to the present or the past. If a member uses objectionable language, he can be called to order after he has used it; but there is no power of foresight given to the Speaker or to a minister to enable him to foretell what a member is about to say. Therefore an objection, to be in order, must have reference to something that has already been said. The right hon. gentleman who leads the House raised the point whether or not an affidavit could be read.
I venture to think that the right hon. gentleman would hardly discuss that question. Every member of this House will admit that an affidavit can be read. It might be of such an utterly improper character that it should not be read, and a member might be called to order for reading it; but that it could be read is, I submit, beyond question. What is the rule to which reference has been made?
No member shall use offensive words against either House or against any member thereof.
That is plain language. It is along the same lines as the law that forbids individuals outside of this House under the pains and penalties of the law to use offensive language against their fellows, for fear it might lead to a breach of the peace. So in this House members are not to use offensive language towards each other for fear that, not a breach of the peace, but a breach of decorum might ensue. What is the meaning of offensive language? Let us assume that a judge sitting on the bench had solemnly given utterance to a judgment which reflected most severely on a member of this House or on a minister. Surely in such a case it could not be said that a member of this House was using offensive words against the member or minister in question if he merely, in the face of the House, read that judgment. Words uttered by a member of this House, as expressing his opinion of another member, would be offensive and out of order; but if a member quoted from a judgment of a judge of the Supreme Court, it is clear that he would not be using offensive words within the meaning of the rule. The only question would be whether he was quoting truly or not. Mr. Justice Cassels in his report, reflected in very strong terms on the administration of several departments, and we know that the head of each department is responsible for the admin-

istration of his department. Any member of this House who quoted from the report of Mr. Justice Cassels was, according to the opinion of the Minister of Public Works, using offensive language towards the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
The report was before parliament.

What difference does that make? The question is the construction of rule 19, and it says nothing about anything being before parliament. In one sense every word uttered in this House to show that hon. gentlemen opposite are not doing their duty may be considered offensive to them; but surely that is not what is meant. If the ruling of the Minister of Public Works now asks for were sustained by the Chair, what would be the result? No judgment or report of a Royal Commission, or a judge could be referred to in this House by any hon. member except under pains and penalties. Therefore, I submit that when the hon.
