not ?
I have declared that no offensive word may be read or spoken in this House against any hon. member. That is rule 19.
Do I understand you to rule, Mr. Speaker
Order.
I am in order, and I will not be put down.

I understand that the hon. member (Mr. McKenzie) asks an explanation; he did not hear my ruling. I have ruled that, under rule 19, no offensive word may be either spoken or read in this House against any hon. member.
That is not the point.
Hear the judge.
I have a perfect right to be heard, and the sneering of the hon.
The affidavit has not been read. But if the affidavit contains any offensive language, it cannot be read.
I submit that it cannot be read.

The point of order, after all the various discussions that have been had, it seems to me narrows down to this: There was a declaration made, it, appears, which apparently reflected upon the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley). The original declaration made a statement to the effect that a certain event had taken place in 1907, that is after the Minister of Public Works became a member of this House. That was objected to by the minister. The date has since been changed, I understand, to read '1905,' which was before the hon. minister became a member of this House. Now, there is a clear distinction between what the House can investigate and what the House cannot investigate as regards a member of this House and as regards a private individual outside this House, and that is plainly laid down by the high authority, May, at page 81:
Libels upon members have also been constantly punished; but to constitute a breach of privilege they must concern the character or conduct of members in that capacity; and as is explained on page 274

And this is the pertinent principle.
-the libel must be based on matters arising in the actual transaction of the business of the House. Aspersions upon the conduct of members as magistrates, or officers in the army or navy, or as counsel, or employers of labour, or in private life, or otherwise than in relation to parliament, are within the cognizance of the courts and are not fit subjects for complaints to the House of Commons.
The moment it appears that this is a charge having reference to something that happened during the private life of the Minister of Public Works, and that the statement about to be read contains grave reflections upon him-and that has been stated by two members of this House-it is taken without the scope of this House and relegated to the courts and is not a fit subject for inquiry here.

I might agree, in what has been so well said by the hon. member (Mr. Sutherland), if we both knew what was the motion to be brought before you. But I have as much right to assume that this is a motion to take steps to get back money that was wrongfully obtained from the public as the hon. member has to assume that it is a motion against the Minister of Public Works. I gather-I do not know whether from something read by you, Mr. Speaker, ot from some words spoken by hon. members-that the main object of the motion is to get back money that belongs to the people. If so, I imagine you cannot prevent it by drawing the herring across the trail by saying that the character of a member of this House is involved. It is a serious question, one which

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lancaster) will allow me; it would be perfectly in order to ask by this motion for an investigation into such a matter. But what is not allowed is to use offensive words in support of the motion, unless the hon. member from St. John city (Mr. Daniel) assumes to make a direct charge in the usual way.

I quite agree with what has been said in that respect, but I am going to point out what it may lead to. No hon. member of this House can expect members to vote for a motion for an investigation without giving some evidence in support of his motion. If he brings that evidence before the House in the form of an affidavit duly sworn to, is he to mutilate that document by cutting out certain words or by changing certain words of the deponent? Is he to say: I have evidence showing that money has been wrongfully obtained from the people by somebody, but, in presenting that evidence as given under oath, I must garble it? Because the reputation of some particular person is involved? We must be practical. If we have the right to get a committee appointed to see whether money belonging to the people has been wrongfully obtained by an individual and should be paid back, surely that right cannot be denied simply because my character or that of anybody else in this House is involved?	,
Then, why have not you the courage of your convictions and make a specific charge?

Before you make a ruling,
Mr. Speaker
Order.

I desire order, Mr. Speaker. Before you make a ruling, I wish to put in this plea: As I understand the ruling, it is that no language can be read
or spoken in this House which is offensive to any member. If I am wrong, I hope you will correct me, Mr. Speaker. Now, I want the House to think about that for a moment as to the absolute revolution in parliamentary practice it may involve and the powers the House of Commons will possess hereafter if that becomes the permanent rule of this Chamber. For instance, suppose that, in carrying out my duty as a member of parliament, I make an investigation into some branches of the Marine and Fisheries Department, and suppose I find that there has been malversation of funds, the paying of bonuses, the taking of presents-suppose that I find that a dozen things that are wrong have been done. And suppose that I get affidavits to prove this. And suppose that one of these solemn declarations sets forth that an officer of the government, it may be a minister of the Crown
No, no.

An officer of the government, it may be a minister of the Crown, was cognizant of these proceedings. I cannot say to the man who is prepared to give me an affidavit setting forth the facts: Cut out this word, or do not use that word. He must make his affidavit, for it is his statement and he is swearing to it. I bring that affidavit into the House and upon that-
Make a charge.

'Make a charge,' my hon. friend says. Let me make my own statement. I put the facts before the House, reading the affidavits and I ask the House to appoint a committee to inquire into the whole matter. As I make my statement I must read the bases upon which I make it, and one of those bases is the affidavit. When I make my statement I am at perfect liberty to show that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, or the Minister of Public Works, has been lax, has lacked foresight, has lacked direction; I can go on and say that he has lacked in fair and honest supervision in the matter. I can make these statements in the House, I think I can make them the basis for asking for an investigation committee. The rules of the House allow that. Under the present ruling that is proposed by the Speaker, I ask you where you would be with reference to investigating anything, and where an opportunity would have any locus standi. Now when you come to read this resolution you will find that it is a resolution asking for the appointment of a commission for a specific purpose; that specific purpose is to look into and make an investigation under oath, get witnesses and bring documents. Investigation into what? Investigation into certain transactions whereby a contract was

got from this government, and whereby a person who was outside the contract entirely, got a rake-off, as we call it, of five cents per cubic yard. That is what is to be looked into, and that is all that is to be looked into.
Order.

Now, let us be quiet for
a moment whilst I state what takes place, according to the affidavit.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If it be a motion as to whether there has been a rake-off, is it not a fact that the motion would be just as complete without any reference to the Minister of Public Works?
Mr- FOSTER. The reference is not to the Minister of Public Works. Now, we have heard a lot about that affidavit. All men are fallible, the Prime Minister and myself not excluded.
That is a belated admission on the part of the hon. gentlemen.

All men are fallible; Mr. Mayes made an affidavit which he swore to, and which affidavit was read in the city of bt. John on the 12th of October. In that affidavit was the date 1907 instead of 1905, as Mr. Mayes declared it was his intention to make it. We will say for the sake ol argument that it was read as 1907. An attempt was made at that meeting to have Uie date corrected and make it 1905. But it was read 1907, and so it came out. The Minister of Public Works says:	That is
absolutely false with reference to myself; it was in 1907 that I was Minister of Public Works, and in 1907 that thing did not take place. But just as soon as the affidavit was published the man who made it, and who ought to have knowledge, made the correction, and said, 1907 is wrong; I did not mean 1907, I meant 1905. Now, was that or was that not the fact? I appeal now to the Prime Minister. He can read the documents and see for himself. I myself, in the city of Toronto, read in the papers of the 13th, the next morning, that Mr. Mayes himself had made the correction, and said that he meant 1905.
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order; the hon. gentleman has spoken twice before.
I wish to finish my statement with reference to the point of order.
I think the member for North Toronto is speaking now with the consent of the House.
He is not speaking to the point of order.
The House must either proceed with this matter or not. My ruling has already been given. But as this

is a matter which may affect any member of the House to-morrow, I want to apply rule 19, which says:
No member shall use offensive words against either House, or against any member thereof-nor speak beside the question in debate.
The moment offensive words are read to me by any hon. gentleman I shall have to stop him. They may be read in a public meeting at St. John, but they cannot be read here, without the hon. gentleman assuming the responsibility thereof, as a matter of public procedure. He cannot lay a charge against the Minister of Public Works without assuming responsibility therefor.
What responsibility?
The responsibility of the member himself, speaking from his seat in the House.
Has any one assumed to lay a charge against the Minister of Public Works here to-day?
I understand the amendment contains one.
The charge was made against a former Minister of Public Works, and not against the gentleman who got the contract. There was no charge made against Mr. Pugsley the private member whatever.

When I was cut into by my hon. friend over there, I was going on to show what were the facts of the case. I was showing that an error had been made by Mr. Mayes; Mr. Mayes corrected that error, as I said, on the 13th, when the affidavit was originally read on the 12th.
I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman has already spoken once, and I for one object to him speaking again.
Order, order.
Several points of order have been taken. I think the hon. member for North Toronto is speaking now on a matter in which the House is interested.
I for one object. The hon. gentleman should not speak oftener than the rules of the House allow. He has no right to speak twice.

I think the member for North Toronto is in order. Several points of order have been raised, I have not kept a record of them. A number of members have spoken, and it seems to be the sense of the House that the hon. member for North Toronto should be privileged to speak again.
No, no.
That is where I raise the point of order. The hon. gentleman has no right to speak twice on the. same subject. If he raises another point of order-
Order, order.
I cannot say that the hon. member for North Toronto has spoken 8n this particular point of order.
We want to know what he is speaking about. I for one want to know what he is speaking about.

All I have to say now is that if we aTe really a parliament and not a madhouse, let us make up our mind which we are. I leave the whole matter in the hands of the right hon. gentleman who leads the House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It certainly devolves upon me as leader of the House to give my opinion on this matter. It is a duty which is not always pleasant, but it is a duty which we have to discharge. At all events, we must endeavour on both sides of the House to bring this matter to a conclusion, with a proper sense of the dignity of the House and a proper application of the rules of the House. If I may refer to a past debate of only a few days ago, I said that I should give an example myeelf, and I will give it again. The rule of the House is that no one is allowed to speak disrespectfully of another member. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) the other day put the matter in a more complete form. He said that no member should be allowed to use words which were not only offensive but painful to another member. If we accept that interpretation we should have no difficulty in coming to a conclusion upon this matter. But, there is an exception to the rule that no member is to be spoken of disrespectfully. If a member rises in the House and says:	I charge Mr. So-and-so, a fellow member-that, in itself is offensive, and under such circumstances the rules of the House allow it. But that does not give a member of the House, under ordinary circumstances, the right to speak of another disrespectfully. If he says that, acting under his sense of duty, he brings such and such an accusation against a fellow member he subjects himself to certain conditions and certain penalties. It is expected of him that he shall prove the charge and if he does not he will render himself liable to very grave censure. That has been done on more than one occasion in this House. Taking the cases historically, it was done on the occasion of the Pacific scandal when Mr. Huntingdon, a member of this House, brought a charge against certain members of the administration. It was done at a later date by Mr. Tarte when he brought a charge against a member of the government of that day. It was done on a subsequent occasion by Mr. Edgar when he brought a charge against a member of the government. Upon all these occasions the member was allowed to speak disrespectfully
and offensively of another but it was upon a charge being made. Now, as I understand it, the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Daniel) does not make any charge against my friend and colleague the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley). He wants to bring in a motion to have certain matters investigated in which the public interest is concerned, and, as I understand, by reason of certain transactions which have taken place the public revenue has been defrauded of a certain amount of money.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Very well, my hon. friend has the right to make such a motion. I do not know whether his motion should be granted or not-I express no opinion upon that-I have not heard it- but, if it is in order to have such a motion made and to have such an investigation entered upon, is it allowable to him to make an insinuation against a fellow member? Is it allowable that he should say of a certain member things which are offensive and painful? According to the rule of the House, as I understand the Speaker to lay it down, it is now allowable for him to do so. Certainly, he has the right to say everything that is conducive to the motion which he has in view, that is conducive to the object which he has in view, but I do not think he has the right to say anything offensive of a fellow member. That is the position that I would take. If my hon. friend wants to make a motion to have a certain investigation, or, to use the hon. gentleman's own words, more particularly an investigation into a transaction which it is said took place between Mr. Mayes and Mr. McAvity and which resulted in a certain transaction in the Department of Public Works I think he has a right to make that motion. I do not know whether it would be granted by the House or not, but if this is so, as far as I can see, it does not violate any rule. But, I think we should pause and consider before we acquiesce in the introduction of any matter that is offensive to the Minister of Public Works. The matter is one which is of great importance. Mr. Speaker has taken it into his consideration and he has given his ruling. I think my hon. friend ought to proceed with his speech, keeping in view always the caution which has been given him by the Speaker that it shall contain nothing offensive to a fellow member. Keeping that in view, he has the right to proceed with his motion. But I would appeal to him, to the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) and to the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart), who are old parliamentarians, that if we want to preserve the dignity and respect of this House the well known rule that no

member should speak offensively of another ought to be rigidly maintained.

May I ask the Prime Minister what are we going to do about that affidavit? A man makes an affidavit in which he tells the story showing that the people of this country have been defrauded of their money. Are we going to garble the reading of that affidavit and are the public and the members of this House not to have the benefit of it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If my hon. friend wants to have an investigation made there is no necessity of him reading that affidavit at all.
Then it would be said that there was no evidence of any body having done anything wrong.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No; if the hon. gentleman says he has reason to believe that these things took place from that affidavit he can bring in anything provided it is not offensive to another member. If the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Daniel) believes that the Minister of Public Works has been guilty of improper conduct it is open to him to make a charge against him, but he does not make a charge against him. He says I want to prove that the public revenue has been defrauded to a certain extent. He can bring in any statement provided it does not reflect upon another member of the House.

This is a question with regard to which we have had a good deal of experience in this House. It has been said that a charge to be made against a member of parliament, must be such as to affect the seat of the member in the House, that if he is convicted of it he is to be turned out of the House and that it is a sufficient objection to a charge against a member to say that it does not affect his seat. Any charge made must be made on the personal responsibility of a member. We hear a good deal about personal responsibility. It is a thing of the past. There is no penalty imposed upon a member of parliament for making a charge against another, none except a feeling in the House against a party making a charge which he cannot prove. He is put into what, in the old country, is called Coventry. No member of the House associates with him for making a false charge, but there is no penalty. Look at the position in a case of this kind. There is no charge in the affidavit, which, even if it were 1907, would affect the party's seat in the House
If this took place in 1907 I could not sit in the House.
You were acting i as an attorney in 1905?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: Yes.

Suppose it is | proven up to the hilt that you made an ar' rangement with this contractor and with ' the government of the country by which he 1 was to get an extra price and you divide the money; you were not a member of the House at that time. Had you not a right to make that arrangement with the contractor?
I did not happen to have made it.

It might have been wrong or anything else, but it is nothing upon which a charge might be made against a member of parliament which might affect his seat in the House. The charge, if the other part of the affidavit is true, is something that we have the right to inquire into and which we ought to have the right to inquire if any one, solicitor or contractor, made an arrangement by which a certain sum of money was filched out of the public treasury for what purpose we know not. We have the right to inquire into it, and we have the right to inquire who the individuals were who benefited by it, even if one of those individuals at the present time is the Minister of Public Works. If he was not the Minister of Public Works at the time
At what time?

In 1905; have we not the right to inquire into it? Are we going to abridge and restrict the rights of this parliament because it may be said that something is offensive to a member of parliament? The idea of urging rule 19 against the introduction of an affidavit of this kind is absurd. The rule says:
Nor use offensive words against either House, or against any member thereof.
It is not an offensive word against a member of the House. Even if everything is true that is in the affidavit it does not come within the description of language contained in the rule. ' Offensive words ' means statements made in the House reflecting upon the character or honour of a member of parliament. This does not come within that category at all. This is a childish objection to the introduction of the affidavit which has been repeated in the House again and again. The minister says that the affidavit which was read in the city of St. John bore the date 1907, and that it was a reflection on him as a minister at the time because he was then the minister. The correction has been made again and again. It is childsh; it is boyish; it is babyish! The affidavit has been corrected.
It may sound all right to my hon. friend, but I would not think it all right.
But the affidavit has been corrected. It was corrected on the floor of the House in which it was read.
No, Sir, and it was published broadcast throughout Canada.
I will take the statement of the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Daniel), who says he was there, and on his honour states that it was 1905 that was mentioned.
Does the hon. gentleman state that he was there?
Yes.
He has said that he was there over and over again.
I have the statement of half a dozen people who were there and it was read 1907.
Talk about the rules of the House! My hon. friend gets up and says that he was "there and the Minister of Public Works gets up and questions the accuracy of his statement.
The statement of the hon. gentleman from St. John will have to be accepted.
If the hon. gentleman from St. John tells me he was present-

I have already told you that.
Mr. PUGSLEY-and that he heard the affidavit, I will accept his statement.
Did the hon. minister not hear me say that I was at that meeting and hear the affidavit read.

I did not hear my hon. friend say that. I heard the hon. gentleman say there was an attempt made to correct it but I did not understand him to say he was present. Now let me ask the hon. gentleman this question: If it was corrected that night at the meeting how came it to be given to the morning papers in St. John and telegraphed all over the country with the false date to it.
Did the hon. gentleman not hear the hon. member for Toronto say that the correction was made next day in the Toronto papers.
It was made in the evening papers after I had corrected it, but no correction came from Mr. Mayes until after I had made the correction.
Six o'clock. Mr. FOSTER. Just one moment.
Six o'clock.
Just one moment if the House will allow me.
Six o'clock.

I appeal to the Prime Minister now. I want to ask the Prime Minister and the House not to consider such a decision made as the Speaker has intimated he will make. It won't harm us to think this matter over until we meet here another time. It is so grave that I do not want to see it go as the Speaker has intimated it is possible it will go.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker has given no such ruling as I understand.
No.

Might I ask the Prime Minister one question. He said it becomes a matter of imperative duty to maintain the dignity of this House; does he not think it is equally important to maintain the privileges of this House?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Certainly.
At six o'clock the House adjourned.

Thursday, April 15, 1909.
